analysis.one_liner: Makes plastic and beverage producers pay to collect, recycle, and clean up their packaging, and phases down single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make the companies that produce packaging and beverage containers responsible for paying to collect, recycle, and clean them up, instead of leaving those costs mostly to taxpayers and local governments. It would set targets to cut single-use plastic over time, create a nationwide deposit of at least 10 cents on drink containers, require minimum recycled content in plastic bottles, and ban a list of toxic chemicals (such as PFAS and phthalates) from beverage containers. It would also limit pollution discharge from plastic pellet facilities, add protections for communities near plastics plants, and explicitly exclude burning or chemically converting plastic from counting as "recycling."
analysis.who_benefits: People living near plastics and petrochemical plants, communities whose waterways and food chains absorb plastic pollution, and local governments that currently pay most of the bill for managing packaging waste. Consumers would get a nationwide bottle-deposit system with guaranteed redemption centers, and the recycling, composting, and reuse industries would gain a large new funding stream from producer fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near plastics plants, local taxpayers, recyclers

how_it_helps.text: Shifts the cost of collecting, recycling, composting, and cleaning up packaging and beverage containers from local governments and ratepayers to the producers that make the products, with producer fees that cannot be shown to consumers as a separate line item on receipts.

Sets binding source-reduction targets for single-use plastics — at least 25% below the 2024 baseline by 2032, 40% by 2040, and 50% by 2050 — with required shifts toward reusable and refillable packaging.
Creates a national beverage container deposit of at least 10 cents, requiring retailers to take returns and producers to fund redemption centers open at least 10 hours a day, six days a week.

Bans toxic substances — including PFAS, phthalates, bisphenols, and halogenated flame retardants — from single-use beverage containers and requires rising minimum recycled content in plastic bottles, from 15% in 2025 to 60% by 2040.

Adds environmental justice protections for communities near covered facilities, limits wastewater and runoff discharges of plastic pellets from production and molding plants, and excludes incineration, pyrolysis, gasification, and other chemical conversion processes from the definition of "recycling."

analysis.who_pays: Producers of packaging, food service products, and beverage containers — especially the petrochemical companies that make plastic resin, the beverage companies that bottle drinks, and consumer goods brands — would pay fees to producer-run organizations, fund the deposit system, and redesign products to meet recycled-content and source-reduction targets. Producers with under $1 million in annual revenue and those making under a ton of product a year are exempt.

drawbacks.text: Producer fees and redesign costs would eventually flow into the price of everyday packaged goods and drinks, even though the bill bars charging them as a separate fee line on a receipt.

The national deposit system adds friction: consumers pay deposits up front and must return containers, small retailers can refuse more than 50 returns per customer per day, and redemption infrastructure takes time to build.

The bill requires every producer to join Producer Responsibility Organizations — nonprofits governed by the producers themselves — and exempts their coordinating activities from antitrust laws, concentrating control of the recycling system in the hands of the largest brands.

The definition of "recyclable" is demanding (materials must be collected under programs covering at least 60% of the U.S. population and meet strict design standards), which could disqualify packaging that some existing community programs currently handle.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes on the largest source of plastic waste at its root and moves a real cost off of taxpayers and onto the companies that create the packaging, with strong provisions on toxic chemicals and on stopping the industry's practice of counting burning plastic as recycling. The honest cost is money: compliance costs would reach consumers through higher prices, and the producer-run organization structure gives the biggest brands a government-sanctioned, antitrust-exempt role in running the system. The environmental gains are broad and long-term; the price effects would be felt at every cash register.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on October 25, 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley and 11 colleagues (10 Democrats and 1 independent) introduced the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act of 2023 in the Senate on October 25, 2023.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

No further action was ever taken: the bill remained in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025, without a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or companion action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of plastic resin, packaging, and beverages keep the status quo, in which taxpayers and local governments bear most of the cost of managing and cleaning up plastic waste, and no new recycled-content or toxic-chemical requirements take effect.

against.name: American Chemistry Council and allied plastics and packaging industry groups

against.what_they_did: Have actively opposed this bill and its earlier versions, which would impose source-reduction, recycled-content, and discharge requirements on their members.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original sponsors were Democrats or one independent, and no Republican cosponsored the bill; it then died without any recorded vote in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill sets source-reduction targets for single-use plastics, mandates rising recycled content, limits plastic pellet discharges into waterways, and refuses to count pyrolysis, gasification, and incineration as recycling — cutting into the industry's core growth market for virgin plastic. Ordinary people gain cleaner water, air, and food chains; the industry's gain comes from avoiding those rules.

Producers would have to fund a nationwide deposit of at least 10 cents, pay refunds, finance redemption centers, meet recycled-content minimums of 15% to 60% in plastic bottles, and show 95% return rates to claim their packaging is refillable. The costs land on producers, with the convenience returning to consumers.

Every covered producer must join producer-run Producer Responsibility Organizations and pay fees that finance the entire collection and recycling system — a real cost, but one that also locks these companies in as the permanent, EPA-approved managers of America's recycling system, with an exemption from antitrust laws for their coordination.

Producer fees would fund collection, sorting, composting, reuse-and-refill infrastructure, and the development of end markets for recycled materials, and organizations are directed to use and fund existing recycling and composting operations.

Retailers must accept returns and handle deposits during business hours, adding workload, though producers reimburse the refund amounts; small stores can cap returns at 50 per customer per day, and retailers are not the ones paying the underlying fees.
